passages.title: CAW Legal Services Plan
passages.text:
The Canadian Auto Workers’ (CAW) Legal Services Plan, designed to give active and retired autoworkers and their families access to totally prepaid or partially reimbursed legal services, has been in operation since late 1985. Plan members have the option of using either the plan’s staff lawyers, whose services are fully covered by the cost of membership in the plan, or an outside lawyer. Outside lawyers, in turn, can either sign up with the plan as a “cooperating lawyer” and accept the CAW’s fee schedule as payment in full, or they can charge a higher fee and collect the balance from the client. Autoworkers appear to have embraced the notion of prepaid legal services: 45 percent of eligible union members were enrolled in the plan by 1988. Moreover, the idea of prepaid legal services has been spreading in Canada. A department store is even offering a plan to holders of its credit card.

While many plan members seem to be happy to get reduced-cost legal help, many lawyers are concerned about the plan’s effect on their profession, especially its impact on prices for legal services. Some point out that even though most lawyers have not joined the plan as cooperating lawyers, legal fees in the cities in which the CAW plan operates have been depressed, in some cases to an unprofitable level. The directors of the plan, however, claim that both clients and lawyers benefit from their arrangement. For while the clients get ready access to reduced-price services, lawyers get professional contact with people who would not otherwise be using legal services, which helps generate even more business for their firms. Experience shows, the directors say, that if people are referred to a firm and receive excellent service, the firm will get three to four other referrals who are not plan subscribers and who would therefore pay the firm’s standard rate.

But it is unlikely that increased use of such plans will result in long-term client satisfaction or in a substantial increase in profits for law firms. Since lawyers with established reputations and client bases can benefit little, if at all, from participation, the plans function largely as marketing devices for lawyers who have yet to establish themselves. While many of these lawyers are no doubt very able and conscientious, they will tend to have less expertise and to provide less satisfaction to clients. At the same time, the downward pressure on fees will mean that the full-fee referrals that proponents say will come through plan participation may not make up for a firm’s investment in providing services at low plan rates. And since lowered fees provide little incentive for lawyers to devote more than minimal effort to cases, a “volume discount” approach toward the practice of law will mean less time devoted to complex cases and a general lowering of quality for clients.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The impact of prepaid legal services plans—specifically the CAW Legal Services Plan—on clients, lawyers, and the legal profession in Canada.

**Framework**

Challenge Position

**Main Point**

While prepaid legal services like the CAW plan have become popular and offer reduced-cost legal help to members, the author argues that these plans are unlikely to provide long-term satisfaction to clients or substantial profits to law firms, and may even lower the quality of legal services overall.
—"But it is unlikely that increased use of such plans will result in long-term client satisfaction or in a substantial increase in profits for law firms." (Start of paragraph 3 is the "Most Valuable Sentence".)

**P1: Introduction to the CAW Legal Services Plan and its Growth**

The first paragraph introduces the CAW Legal Services Plan, which allows autoworkers and their families to access prepaid or partially reimbursed legal services through staff or outside lawyers. The idea has caught on, with a significant portion of union members enrolled and even other sectors experimenting with similar plans.

**P2: Lawyers’ Concerns and Plan Directors’ Counterarguments**

Here we learn that while many plan members are happy with reduced legal costs, many lawyers are worried these plans drive prices down too much. Critics say fees are dropping to unprofitable levels, but plan directors argue that lawyers benefit from increased business and referrals, which supposedly offset discounts.

**P3: Author’s Skepticism—Long-Term Issues and Lowered Quality**

The author pivots here, expressing skepticism about these plans' benefits. They claim that such plans are mainly helpful for lawyers just starting out—not established ones—and that participating lawyers may be less experienced, potentially providing lower-quality service. Low fees can result in lawyers spending minimal time on cases, ultimately hurting both client satisfaction and law firm profitability.

Although they have so far attracted many subscribers, it is doubtful whether the CAW Legal Services Plan and other similar prepaid plans will benefit lawyers and clients in the long run.

questions.prompt: The passage most strongly suggests that, according to proponents of prepaid legal plans, cooperating lawyers benefit from taking clients at lower fees in which one of the following ways?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
If we CTRL + F or scan for "proponents" we'll find that literal word in the 2nd to last sentence of the passage, which alludes to

*the full-fee referrals that proponents say will come through plan participation*

That's saying that, "Participating in the plan will result in full-fee referrals".

Okay, a "cooperating lawyer" is a lawyer participating in the plan. And they'll **benefit** from a full-fee referral? Let's make sure we understand what a full-fee referral is.

The end of the 2nd paragraph was explaining how "both clients and (cooperating) lawyers **benefit** from this (plan's) arrangement."

The lawyers "get professional contact with people who would otherwise not be using legal services ... and if people are referred to a firm and receive excellent service, the firm will get three to four other *referrals* who aren't in the plan and who would therefore pay the firm's *standard rate* (full-fee referral)."

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something like, the lawyers benefit because "even though they work on the cheap for the CAW client, that client is so happy that they refer several other people to the lawyer. These other people aren't in the CAW plan, so they are full-price clients."

choices.text: Lawyers can expect to gain expertise in a wide variety of legal services by availing themselves of the access to diverse clientele that plan participation affords.
choices.explanation:
We're looking for "the clients they help at a discounted rate through the CAW plan will refer the law firm to other people who will then pay full price".

It doesn't have anything to do with gaining expertise in a wide variety of legal services.

choices.text: Experienced cooperating lawyers are likely to enjoy the higher profits of long-term, complex cases, for which new lawyers are not suited.
choices.tag: Unrelated to Goal: experienced vs. new
choices.explanation:
We're looking for "the clients they help at a discounted rate through the CAW plan will refer the law firm to other people who will then pay full price".

It doesn't have anything to do with talking about a distinction between experienced and inexperienced lawyers, as it pertains to longer more complex cases.

choices.text: Lower rates of profit will be offset by a higher volume of clients and new business through word-of-mouth recommendations.
choices.explanation:
We're looking for "the clients they help at a discounted rate through the CAW plan will refer the law firm to other people who will then pay full price".

*Lower rates of profit* = the CAW plan client gets helped at a discounted rate

*offset* = net benefit

*higher volume of clients and new business through word-of-mouth recommendations* = satisfied clients are referring this lawyer to 3 or 4 other people

choices.text: Lower fees tend to attract clients away from established, nonparticipating law firms.
choices.tag: Unrelated to Goal: steal other firms' clients / Contradicted
choices.explanation:
We're looking for "the clients they help at a discounted rate through the CAW plan will refer the law firm to other people who will then pay full price".

This is talking about "giving the CAW clients the discounted rate to lure them away from other firms that are more established".

But this is actually contradicted by the idea that proponents are saying cooperating lawyers who work with CAW clients will "get professional contact with people **who would** ***not*** **otherwise** be using legal services".

The initial clients a lawyer would get through the CAW plan are not clients of any law firm.

choices.text: With all legal fees moving downward to match the plans’ schedules, the profession will respond to market forces.
choices.explanation:
We're looking for "the clients they help at a discounted rate through the CAW plan will refer the law firm to other people who will then pay full price".

It doesn't have anything to do with the industry's pricing benchmarks moving downward from market forces.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately represents the primary function of the author's mention of marketing devices (second sentence of the last paragraph)?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The correct answer to *Local Purpose* questions usually reinforces language from a broader Framing Idea that comes right before the detail in question (or, less commonly, from a broader Takeaway that comes right after it).

The author calls the prepaid legal service plans a "marketing device" in the 2nd sentence of the final paragraph.

What is the framing idea right before it? Well the first sentence of the paragraph announces the main point of the last paragraph:

*It's unlikely that increased use of such plans will result in long-term client satisfaction or in a substantial increase in profits for law firms*.

The author thinks that this won't cause a big increase in profits for participating firms because, "*lawyers with established reputations and client bases can benefit little"* from these plans, so they probably won't partake.

Why won't it result in long-term client satisfaction? Because, "*these plans will largely attract lawyers who have yet to establish themselves, and they will tend to have less expertise and provide less satisfaction to clients."*

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
So we could say that the author refers to these plans as "marketing devices" as part of her broader contention that these plans aren't a good idea. They will put people into contact with less experienced lawyers.

On a more specific level, the author is saying that this plan will be a "marketing device" for inexperienced lawyers who are trying to find clients, because people who sign up for the plan will have to choose from a participating lawyer (and experienced lawyers with clients will not choose to participate).

choices.text: It points to an aspect of legal plans that the author believes will be detrimental to the quality of legal services.
choices.explanation:
This reinforces the "Bookend" ideas, which we love to see on Local Purpose.

Before the author says "marketing plans", she says that these legal plans are unlikely to result in long-term client satisfaction or in an increase in profits for law firms.

After the author says "marketing plans", she explains how working with these inexperienced lawyers will mean working with lawyers who "tend to have less expertise and to provide less satisfaction to clients".

In other words, the fact that these plans will mainly attract inexperienced lawyers means that the quality of legal services provided by these plans will be lower than average (i.e. detrimental to quality).

choices.text: It is identified by the author as one of the primary ways in which plan administrators believe themselves to be contributing materially to the legal profession in return for lawyers’ participation.
choices.tag: Too Strong: primary ways / Wrong Selling Point
choices.explanation:
The author never suggests that plan administrators boast, as one of the primary virtues of these legal plans, that "these will act as marketing devices for inexperienced lawyers!"

The administrators think that they're contributing materially to the legal profession primarily by saying, "If you participate in the plan, then sure you'll end up working for less money when you're dealing with plan clients, but *they* will end up referring you to people not in the plan, so you'll get some full-fee work out of this".

In other words, the primary way that plan administrators think that prepaid legal plans will help lawyers is by helping them get more full-fee clients (who aren't in the plan). The administrators never say, "We think this will help the legal profession by platforming inexperienced lawyers".

The author brings up that issue as a reason for concern with these plans.

choices.text: It identifies what the author considers to be one of the few unequivocal benefits that legal plans can provide.
choices.explanation: The author is talking about "marketing plans" as a bad thing. She thinks that people getting legal services via these plans will primarily be working with less skilled, less experienced lawyers.

choices.text: It is reported as part of several arguments that the author attributes to established lawyers who oppose plan participation.
choices.explanation:
The author is speaking with her own voice in most of this last paragraph, not attributing arguments to other people.

The only moment in the last paragraph where the author attributes an argument to someone else is when she cites an argument that **proponents** of plan participation make.

choices.text: It describes one of the chief burdens of lawyers who have yet to establish themselves and offers an explanation of their advocacy of legal plans.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: explain their advocacy / Detail-Sentence Trap
choices.explanation:
This is a great example of a trap answer on Local Purpose that is too focused on the detail sentence itself, rather than connecting it to bigger, broader adjacent ideas.

The author never cites "need to market oneself" as one of the **chief** burdens of inexperienced lawyers. And she never attempts to explain their advocacy of legal plans. The passage never states that inexperienced lawyers advocate these legal plans. The author is definitely suggesting a reason why they might, but the passage has never said they do, so we can't say our author is trying to explain something that was never mentioned.

passages.title: Historiography
passages.text:
In the field of historiography—the writing of history based on a critical examination of authentic primary information sources—one area that has recently attracted attention focuses on the responses of explorers and settlers to new landscapes in order to provide insights into the transformations the landscape itself has undergone as a result of settlement. In this endeavor historiographers examining the history of the Pacific Coast of the United States have traditionally depended on the records left by European American explorers of the nineteenth century who, as commissioned agents of the U.S. government, were instructed to report thoroughly their findings in writing.

But in furthering this investigation some historiographers have recently recognized the need to expand their definition of what a source is. They maintain that the sources traditionally accepted as documenting the history of the Pacific Coast have too often omitted the response of Asian settlers to this territory. In part this is due to the dearth of written records left by Asian settlers; in contrast to the commissioned agents, most of the people who first came to western North America from Asia during this same period did not focus on developing a self-conscious written record of their involvement with the landscape. But because a full study of a culture’s historical relationship to its land cannot confine itself to a narrow record of experience, these historiographers have begun to recognize the value of other kinds of evidence, such as the actions of Asian settlers.

As a case in point, the role of Chinese settlers in expanding agriculture throughout the Pacific Coast territory is integral to the history of the region. Without access to the better land, Chinese settlers looked for agricultural potential in this generally arid region where other settlers did not. For example, where settlers of European descent looked at willows and saw only useless, untillable swamp, Chinese settlers saw fresh water, fertile soil, and the potential for bringing water to more arid areas via irrigation. Where other settlers who looked at certain weeds, such as wild mustard, generally saw a nuisance, Chinese settlers saw abundant raw material for valuable spices from a plant naturally suited to the local soil and climate.

Given their role in the labor force shaping this territory in the nineteenth century, the Chinese settlers offered more than just a new view of the land. Their vision was reinforced by specialized skills involving swamp reclamation and irrigation systems, which helped lay the foundation for the now well-known and prosperous agribusiness of the region. That 80 percent of the area’s cropland is now irrigated and that the region is currently the top producer of many specialty crops cannot be fully understood by historiographers without attention to the input of Chinese settlers as reconstructed from their interactions with that landscape.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The importance of including Chinese settlers' perspectives and contributions when studying the history of how the Pacific Coast landscape was transformed by settlement.

**Framework**

Old / New

**Main Point**

Recent historiographers argue that to fully understand the transformation of the Pacific Coast's landscape, it's necessary to look beyond traditional written records from European American explorers and include the actions and contributions of Chinese settlers, whose innovative approaches to agriculture reshaped the region. ("...these historiographers have begun to recognize the value of other kinds of evidence, such as the actions of Asian settlers" - P2; "That 80 percent of the area’s cropland is now irrigated and that the region is currently the top producer of many specialty crops cannot be fully understood by historiographers without attention to the input of Chinese settlers..." - P4)

**P1: Traditional Sources for Studying Pacific Coast History**

Historians have usually relied on the detailed written reports from 19th-century European American explorers to study how explorers and settlers responded to the Pacific Coast landscape.

**P2: Reevaluating What Counts as a Source**

Recently, some scholars have pointed out that these traditional records ignore Asian settlers, mostly because there’s a lack of written documents from them. These historians suggest it's important to also look at other kinds of evidence—like settlers' actions—to get a fuller picture.

**P3: Chinese Settlers’ Different Approach to the Land**

The passage gives examples of how Chinese settlers saw agricultural opportunities in places others didn’t, using resources like swamps and wild mustard in innovative ways that differed from European settlers.

**P4: Lasting Impact of Chinese Contributions**

Chinese settlers not only saw the land differently, but they also brought specialized skills in areas like irrigation and swamp reclamation. Their innovations were crucial in shaping the region's agricultural success, and their contributions must be recognized to fully understand the area's history.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of the passage is historiography in relation to the Pacific Coast of the U.S.

Why is the author writing about this topic? What framework did we use?

The first sentence reveals a potential *Old / New* framework. The **New** thing happening in historiography is focusing on the responses of explorers and settlers to new landscapes, as a way of understanding how that landscape was transformed due to settlement.

We might also have considered a *Theme / Example* framework, because the passage tells us this broad trend and then zooms in on a specific manifestation of it, by focusing on the history of the Pacific Coast of the U.S.

The **Old** way of investigating that history was to rely on records left by Euro-American explorers, who were commissioned by the U.S. government.

The **New** way of investigating that history is to "expand the definition of a source" and instead of just looking for documents, recognizing "the value of other kinds of evidence, such as the actions of Asian settlers".

The 3rd paragraph begins with the classic *Theme / Example* indicator, "a case in point".

Does our author express any attitude about this new direction in historiography? Yes she seems to fully support it. In the 2nd paragraph, we see, "a full study of a culture's historical relationship to its land **cannot confine itself** to a narrow record of experience (i.e. whatever documents/records are available)".

And in the final sentence of the passage, "X **cannot be fully understood** by historiographers without attention to the input of Chinese settlers as reconstructed from their interactions with that landscape".

So the big themes we want in the main point answer are things like,
- historiography is expanding its sense of what a source is, going from the Old notion of just looking at documents to the New notion of also looking at the actions of settlers who transformed a landscape.

- when historiographers look at the history of the Pacific Coast U.S., they need to expand their sense of what primary sources are, not just looking at Euro-American documents but also looking at the actions of Asian settlers who transformed that landscape.

choices.text: The history of settlement along the Pacific Coast of the U.S., as understood by most historiographers, is confirmed by evidence reconstructed from the actions of Asian settlers.
choices.tag: Too Strong: most / confirmed / Wrong Emphasis: doesn't address New
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is,

*The history of settlement along the Pacific Coast of the U.S. is confirmed by evidence reconstructed from the actions of Asian settlers.*

The passage never talked about confirming an old view of history.

The passage also never gave us a generalization about how **most** historiographers understood the history of that coast.

We should also be bothered by the fact that the *New* thing in historiography isn't being mentioned at all in this answer.

choices.text: Asian settlers on the Pacific Coast of the U.S. left a record of their experiences that traditional historiographers believed to be irrelevant.
choices.tag: Too Narrow: Asian settlers / Too Strong: irrelevant
choices.explanation:
We don't have any textual support for the strongly worded idea that traditional historiographers thought that the records left by Asian settlers were **irrelevant**.

This answer also doesn't capture the *New* thing in historiography, the *Theme* that is being spotlighted by talking about the Pacific Coast.

There's nothing in here about this new focus on the response of explorers and settlers, about the newfound willingness to consider the actions of settlers to be a primary source.

choices.text: To understand Asian settlers’ impact on the history of the Pacific Coast of the U.S., historiographers have had to recognize the value of nontraditional kinds of historiographic evidence.
choices.explanation:
This is capturing the *New* thing happening in historiography. Traditionally, they would just consider documents and records.

But now there's a willingness to consider the actions and responses of settlers. By applying this new mindset to the history of the Pacific Coast of the U.S., historiographers are better able to capture the impact of Asian settlers on transforming that landscape.

The phrasing of, "to understand the impact, historiographers have **had to recognize** the value of nontraditional evidence" matches up well with our two author tone moments:

*"a full study of a culture's historical relationship to its land **cannot confine itself** to a narrow record of experience"*

*"X **cannot be fully understood** by historiographers without attention to the input of Chinese settlers as reconstructed from their interactions with that landscape".*

choices.text: Spurred by new findings regarding Asian settlement on the Pacific Coast of the U.S., historiographers have begun to debate the methodological foundations of historiography.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: debating foundations / Reversed Causal Relationship
choices.explanation:
The *New* thing going down in historiography is an *expansion* of how they define "a source".

There was nothing in the passage about historiographers **debating** the **foundations** of historiography.

But even if we accept that "recognizing they need to expand their definition of what a source is" means that they're "debating the methodological foundations" of their field, we can't support the causal claim this answer makes.

This answer says that "there were new findings regarding Asian settlements on the Pacific U.S. Coast" and those new findings **caused** the historiographers to expand their definition of what a source is.

But the causal relationship in the passage is the reverse. Spurred by an expanded definition of what a source is, historiographers were able to uncover new findings about Asian settlers on the Pacific U.S. Coast.

choices.text: By examining only written information, historiography as it is traditionally practiced has produced inaccurate historical accounts.
choices.tag: Wrong Emphasis: missing Pacific Coast / Out of Scope: inaccurate accounts / Too Strong: only
choices.explanation:
Every paragraph of the passage talks about the Pacific Coast of the U.S. But the main point answer doesn't reference it at all? That's fishy.

We also don't have support for the strongly worded claim that historiography in the past has examined **only** written information.

And the author nowhere says that historiography has produced inaccurate historical accounts (although the author would probably say that their account of the Pacific Coast had so far been "incomplete").

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's primary purpose in discussing Chinese settlers in the third paragraph?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Normally when they ask us about the purpose of a specific detail or example, it's *to illustrate the broader claim that was said* *****right before***** *it.*

The third paragraph begins with the phrase ****"As a case in point****", so we know that the author is discussing the Chinese settlers as an example of whatever was said at the end of the 2nd paragraph.

That final sentence of the 2nd paragraph is saying, "If you want to fully study a culture's historical relationship to its land, you can't confine yourself to [only looking at the scarce written records of Asian settlers of the time]. You have to consider other things, like the *actions* of these Asian settlers."

So the 3rd paragraph should be an example of Asian settlers whose *actions* tell us something about their culture's historical relationship to the land.

Indeed, the 3rd paragraph talks about actions like growing wild mustard for the sake of spices, and using swamp water to irrigate other areas. These actions were integral to the expansion of agriculture across the Pacific Coast.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Look for something reinforcing language from the sentence that ends the 2nd paragraph:

The Chinese settlers were discussed as an example of valuable historical insight you can gain when you recognize the value of other kinds of evidence, such as the *actions* of Asian settlers.

choices.text: to suggest that Chinese settlers followed typical settlement patterns in this region during the nineteenth century
choices.tag: Too Strong: typical / Out of Scope: settlement patterns
choices.explanation: The passage doesn't discuss any settlement patterns, nor does it say that the Chinese settlers were following a ****typical**** pattern.

choices.text: to argue that little written evidence of Chinese settlers’ practices survives
choices.tag: Weaker Match: Wrong Half of Target Sentence
choices.explanation:
We're looking for an answer that sounds like the final sentence of the 2nd paragraph, but the final sentence of the 2nd paragraph actually has two separate claims:

1. *Because* a full study cannot confine itself to the little written evidence we have of Chinese settlers' practices,
2. Historiographers are seeing the value in recognizing other kinds of evidence, such as the actions of Asian settlers

This answer choice is saying that the 3rd paragraph is trying to convince us of #1, that there isn't much written evidence. But the 3rd paragraph is supporting #2.

choices.text: to provide examples illustrating the unique view Asian settlers had of the land
choices.explanation:
This correct answer reinforces the last sentence of the 2nd paragraph, in the sense that it acknowledges that the 3rd paragraph, which is about Chinese settlers, was used as ****a case in point**** for a generalization made about Asian settlers more broadly.

The language about "illustrating their unique view" matches up with the first sentence of the 4th paragraph, which says "The Chinese settlers offered more than just ****a new view of the land****."

The examples in the 3rd paragraph certainly qualify as illustrations of Chinese (thus, Asian) settlers having an innovative outlook on the potential of the environment.

choices.text: to demonstrate that the history of settlement in the region has become a point of contention among historiographers
choices.explanation:
*Contentious* discussions are heated, argumentative discussions. "A point of contention" is used in milder contexts like negotiations, but it still indicates a gridlocked disagreement.

We don't have any support for the idea that historiographers are fighting over the settlements; they're just collectively broadening their sense of what a source can be.

choices.text: to claim that the historical record provided by the actions of Asian settlers is inconsistent with history as derived from traditional sources
choices.explanation: There's nothing in the final sentence of the 2nd paragraph (or in the 3rd paragraph) that says the actions of the Asian settlers ****contradict**** history as derived from traditional sources.

questions.prompt: The passage states that the primary traditional historiographic sources of information about the history of the Pacific Coast of the U.S. have which one of the following characteristics?

choices.text: They were written both before and after Asian settlers arrived in the area.
They include accounts by Native Americans in the area.
They are primarily concerned with potential agricultural uses of the land.
They focus primarily on the presence of water sources in the region.
They are accounts left by European American explorers.

questions.prompt: The author would most likely disagree with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Most *Opinion* questions with no keywords have a pretty *Undefined Target*, because we could be tested on anything the author said throughout the passage.

But if the author's **opinion** doesn't seem to show up much in the passage, then sometimes we can constrain where we look a bit.

In this passage, the first two paragraphs all read very neutral. We don't really hear the author's voice until the end of the 2nd paragraph, where she is implicitly agreeing with historiographers.

She, like they, recognize that "a full study of a culture's historical relationship to its land cannot confine itself to a narrow record of experience".

The final sentence of the passage reiterates this sentiment, as it applies to the Chinese settlers: "That the area [now looks the way it does] cannot be fully understood by historiographers without attention to the input of Chinese settlers' interactions with that landscape."

The rest of the author's voice is found in the 3rd and 4th paragraph, where she mainly stresses with a fair degree of respect and admiration how Chinese settlers had special insights into the landscape and skillsets with which to manipulate the landscape.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Since this is asking what the author would *Disagree* with, the incorrect answers could sound like something our author would endorse or they could just sound like something the author didn't talk about.

The correct answer should be something that actively goes against something our author thinks.

choices.text: Examining the actions not only of Asian settlers but of other cultural groups of the Pacific Coast of the U.S. is necessary to a full understanding of the impact of settlement on the landscape there.
choices.explanation:
This answer choice sounds a ton like the final sentence in the passage.

That final sentence only talks about needing to appreciate the input of **Chinese settlers**. It doesn't mention that examining any other cultural group would be necessary.

But our author definitely thinks that historiographers shouldn't confine themselves to a narrow record of experience.

If historiographers **only** looked at Asian settlers, then they would ignore all the actions of the European American explorers. The author certainly isn't going to advocate that. She wants historiographers to take into account every group's influence in order to get a full understanding.

choices.text: The significance of certain actions to the writing of history may be recognized by one group of historiographers but not another.
choices.explanation:
This is very hard to disagree with because it's so softly worded ("may be").

In order to pick this answer, we'd have to support the idea that in the author's mind, "every group of historiographers will recognize the same set of actions as significant and the same set of actions as insignificant."

If there is ever ANY action where one group would say "significant" and another group would say "not significant", then this answer is true.

In addition to the fact that no person would ever disagree with a statement this mild, we have the context from the early part of the 2nd paragraph where it's saying, "in furthering this investigation, **some** historiographers have recently recognized the need to expand their definition of what a source is. The sources **traditionally accepted** as documenting the history have **too often omitted** the response of Asian settlers to this territory."

It sounds like there's some disagreement among historiographers over whether the actions of the Asian settlers are significant.

choices.text: Recognizing the actions of Asian settlers adds to but does not complete the writing of the history of the Pacific Coast of the U.S.
choices.explanation:
It's easy to support that the author thinks "recognizing the actions of Asian settlers adds to the writing of the history of Pacific Coast U.S."

The 3rd paragraph starts with "as a case in point", which is signaling that the author thinks the story of the Asian settlers is an example of something you need to know to have a full understanding of Pacific Coast history.

The final sentence of the passage also echoes this.

We don't have any support sentence for the idea that "the actions of the Asian settlers does not complete the writing of the history", but it would be pretty extreme to disagree with that.

Disagreeing with that would mean that you believe, "Now that we've recognized the actions of the Asian settlers, we are 100% done with writing the history of the Pacific U.S. It's complete."

choices.text: By recognizing as evidence the actions of people, historiographers expand the definition of what a source is.
choices.explanation: The first two sentences of the 2nd paragraph support this. "Some historiographers have recognized the need to *expand* their definition of a source; they maintain that we've traditionally omitted the response (actions) of Asian settlers to this territory".

choices.text: The expanded definition of a source will probably not be relevant to studies of regions that have no significant immigration of non-Europeans.
choices.explanation:
This goes against the last sentence of the 2nd paragraph, where the author is agreeing with historiographers who have started to recognize the truth:

*a full study of a culture's historical relationship to its land cannot confine itself to a narrow record of experience, such as the actions of Asian settlers* (which the beginning of the 2nd paragraph tells us is an expanded definition of a source).

Nothing in that general language suggests that expanding our definition of a source is only relevant for certain types of cultures. The author seems to appreciate the underlying logic of studying the actions of settlers who may not have left any written record, but whose actions still deeply inform the history of the region.

That would apply to any such situation; it's not contingent on the percentage of non-Europeans immigrants.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, each of the following was an aspect of Chinese settlers' initial interactions with the landscape of the Pacific Coast of the U.S. EXCEPT:

choices.text: new ideas for utilizing local plants
a new view of the land
specialized agricultural skills
knowledge of agribusiness practices
knowledge of irrigation systems

questions.prompt: Which one of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

choices.text: Most Chinese settlers came to the Pacific Coast of the U.S. because the climate was similar to that with which they were familiar.
Chinese agricultural methods in the nineteenth century included knowledge of swamp reclamation.
Settlers of European descent used wild mustard seed as a spice.
Because of the abundance of written sources available, it is not worthwhile to examine the actions of European settlers.
What written records were left by Asian settlers were neglected and consequently lost to scholarly research.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to strengthen the author's main claim in the last sentence of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
When a question stem says we have to strengthen / weaken an ****argument****, then we need to think about the author's conclusion and evidence.

But if it just says to strengthen / weaken a claim or hypothesis, then we don't really have to read much more than that claim.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
The author's final claim is that "You won't fully understand why this area has so much irrigated cropland or why it produces many specialty crops unless you appreciate the contributions of Chinese settlers."

We could rephrase that as, "Chinese settlers were crucial to why this area now has so much irrigated cropland and why it produces many specialty crops."

An answer doesn't necessarily have to talk about both. If it helps us see the connection between Chinese settlers and irrigation or between specialty crops, it's helping to support that claim.

choices.text: Market research of agribusinesses owned by descendants of Chinese settlers shows that the market for the region’s specialty crops has grown substantially faster than the market for any other crops in the last decade.
choices.explanation:
This seems to be a fact more about the present than about connecting the past to the present.

We need to hear that the Chinese settlers did stuff that set this region up for irrigation / specialty crop success.

This answer is just saying that presently the specialty crop market is having success, for descendants of these Chinese settlers. But the answer isn't telling us anything that makes the Chinese settlers sound like they did anything crucial.

choices.text: Nineteenth-century surveying records indicate that the lands now cultivated by specialty crop businesses owned by descendants of Chinese settlers were formerly swamp lands.
choices.explanation:
The fact that the current specialty crop businesses (that connect back to the Chinese settlers) are on land that started out as swamp lands suggests that when Chinese settlers arrived, they turned that land from swamp land into specialty crop territory.

We were told at the end of the 3rd paragraph that,
*where Europeans saw useless, untillable swamp, Chinese settlers saw fresh water, fertile soil, and the potential for bringing water via irrigation.*

So if we connect the dots, the Chinese settlers "interacted with that landscape" by bringing water in via irrigation and turning that land into useful, tillable soil for growing specialty crops.

Hence, they did something crucial to turn this area into the top producer of many specialty crops, and so you can't fully understand why this area is now the top producer of many specialty crop without appreciating how these Chinese settlers interacted with that landscape.

choices.text: Research by university agricultural science departments proves that the formerly arid lands now cultivated by large agribusinesses contain extremely fertile soil when they are sufficiently irrigated.
choices.explanation: Nothing in this answer tells us anything that connects to the Chinese settlers, so it's not helping us to argue that they interacted with the landscape in some crucial manner that paved the way for irrigation / specialty crops.

choices.text: A technological history tracing the development of irrigation systems in the region reveals that their efficiency has increased steadily since the nineteenth century.
choices.explanation:
Nothing in this answer tells us anything that connects to the Chinese settlers.

The Chinese settlers did come to the Pacific Coast area in the 19th century, but we'd be adding a big speculative leap to attribute this answer to *them* simply because of that. European explorers also arrived in the 19th century.

choices.text: Weather records compiled over the previous century demonstrate that the weather patterns in the region are well-suited to growing certain specialty crops as long as they are irrigated.
choices.explanation: Nothing in this answer tells us anything that connects to the Chinese settlers, so it's not helping us to argue that they interacted with the landscape in some crucial manner that paved the way for irrigation / specialty crops.

passages.title: NGF
passages.text:
The survival of nerve cells, as well as their performance of some specialized functions, is regulated by chemicals known as neurotrophic factors, which are produced in the bodies of animals, including humans. Rita Levi-Montalcini’s discovery in the 1950s of the first of these agents, a hormonelike substance now known as NGF, was a crucial development in the history of biochemistry, which led to Levi-Montalcini sharing the Nobel Prize for medicine in 1986.

In the mid-1940s, Levi-Montalcini had begun by hypothesizing that many of the immature nerve cells produced in the development of an organism are normally programmed to die. In order to confirm this theory, she conducted research that in 1949 found that, when embryos are in the process of forming their nervous systems, they produce many more nerve cells than are finally required, the number that survives eventually adjusting itself to the volume of tissue to be supplied with nerves. A further phase of the experimentation, which led to Levi-Montalcini’s identification of the substance that controls this process, began with her observation that the development of nerves in chick embryos could be stimulated by implanting a certain variety of mouse tumor in the embryos. She theorized that a chemical produced by the tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth. To investigate this hypothesis, she used the then new technique of tissue culture, by which specific types of body cells can be made to grow outside the organism from which they are derived. Within twenty-four hours, her tissue cultures of chick embryo extracts developed dense halos of nerve tissue near the places in the culture where she had added the mouse tumor. Further research identified a specific substance contributed by the mouse tumors that was responsible for the effects Levi-Montalcini had observed: a protein that she named “nerve growth factor” (NGF).

NGF was the first of many cell-growth factors to be found in the bodies of animals. Through Levi-Montalcini’s work and other subsequent research, it has been determined that this substance is present in many tissues and biological fluids, and that it is especially concentrated in some organs. In developing organisms, nerve cells apparently receive this growth factor locally from the cells of muscles or other organs to which they will form connections for transmission of nerve impulses, and sometimes from supporting cells intermingled with the nerve tissue. NGF seems to play two roles, serving initially to direct the developing nerve processes toward the correct, specific “target” cells with which they must connect, and later being necessary for the continued survival of those nerve cells. During some periods of their development, the types of nerve cells that are affected by NGF—primarily cells outside the brain and spinal cord—die if the factor is not present or if they encounter anti-NGF antibodies.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The discovery and role of nerve growth factor (NGF) and neurotrophic factors in nerve cell survival and development.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy (with a touch of Answer / Explain—explaining how NGF works and why it's important)

**Main Point**

Rita Levi-Montalcini’s discovery of nerve growth factor (NGF) was a landmark achievement that explained how nerve cells survive, develop, and connect, revealing the key role of neurotrophic factors in animal biology. (The Most Valuable Sentence: The first paragraph’s closing sentence: “Rita Levi-Montalcini’s discovery in the 1950s of the first of these agents, a hormonelike substance now known as NGF, was a crucial development in the history of biochemistry, which led to Levi-Montalcini sharing the Nobel Prize for medicine in 1986.”)

**P1: Introduction to Neurotrophic Factors and Levi-Montalcini’s Discovery**

We’re introduced to neurotrophic factors—special chemicals that help nerve cells survive and work. Rita Levi-Montalcini discovered the first important one (NGF), which forever changed how scientists thought about nerve cells and earned her a Nobel Prize.

**P2: The Experiments and Discovery of NGF**

Levi-Montalcini thought lots of nerve cells were meant to die off during development, and she found evidence for this in embryos. Noticing that mouse tumors caused unusual nerve growth in chick embryos, she guessed a chemical from the tumors was responsible. By using tissue cultures, she proved that a specific protein produced by the tumors—NGF—was making this happen.

**P3: The Function and Importance of NGF**

NGF turned out to be the first of many such growth factors in animals. Thanks to Levi-Montalcini’s work and later research, scientists now know NGF helps nerve cells not just grow, but also survive and connect to the right targets during development. If nerve cells don’t get NGF, they can’t survive, which makes this protein crucial for healthy nervous systems, especially outside the brain and spinal cord.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of this passage was Levi-Montalcini's discovery of NGF.

Why was the author writing about it? What framework did we use?

Since the passage mainly tells a chronological, factual story, we would use *Highlight Noteworthy*. That means our main point idea will be a moment where the author tells us why this topic he's writing about is important or distinctive, or it will be some sort of framing idea that the rest of the passage unpacks.

This passage seems more like the former, as the first paragraph ends by saying this was, "a **crucial** development in the history of biochemistry ... it won her the Nobel Prize".

And the passage ends by summing up the aftermath/impact of her discovery.

Let's look for something like, "Levi-Montalcini's discovery of NGF, the first neurotrophic factors was a crucial development in the history of biochemistry that led to many other cell-growth factors being found".

choices.text: Levi-Montalcini’s discovery of neurotrophic factors as a result of research carried out in the 1940s was a major contribution to our understanding of the role of naturally occurring chemicals, especially NGF, in the development of chick embryos.
choices.explanation:
This answer feels very close, because the main clause is saying, "Her discovery was a major contribution to our understanding".

But she is noteworthy for how she contributed to our understanding of neurotrophic factors and other cell-growth factors, not to our understanding of "natural chemicals in the development of chick embryos".

Her work on chick embryos led her to discover NGF, and NGF was mind-blowing on a much broader scale to the field of biochemistry. It wasn't because of what it was specifically saying about chick embryos (these neurotrophic factors she opened our eyes to occur in all animals, including humans).

choices.text: Levi-Montalcini’s discovery of NGF, a neurotrophic factor that stimulates the development of some types of nerve tissue and whose presence or absence in surrounding cells helps determine whether particular nerve cells will survive, was a pivotal development in biochemistry.
choices.explanation:
This main clause better matches the end of the 1st sentence, where the author is putting a stamp on why Levi-Montalcini is noteworthy:

*Her discovery of NGF was a pivotal development in biochemistry*.

This answer choice has so much fluff in between the Subject and the Verb of the main clause, it's a really good example of why we practice initially just reading the main clause on Main Point answers.

Once we feel good about the main clause, we have to sign off on all the details.

*Is* NGF a neurotrophic factor that stimulates the development of some types of nerve tissue? Yes. She found that she could stimulate the development of nerves in chick embryos by implanting tumors that contained NGF.

*Is* NGF something whose presence or absence in surrounding cells helps determine whether nerve cells will survive?

Yes, "NGF seems to play two roles -- serving initially to direct the developing nerve processes toward the correct target cells, and later being necessary for the continued survival of those cells".

choices.text: NGF, which is necessary for the survival and proper functioning of nerve cells, was discovered by Levi-Montalcini in a series of experiments using the technique of tissue culture, which she devised in the 1940s.
choices.explanation:
This is somewhat tempting, but it just tells us the small story about what Levi-Montalcini did, without giving us the larger importance or ramification of that story.

The main clause is,

*NGF was discovered by Levi-Montalcini in a series of experiments using tissue culture*.

Okay, that seems true. But why is that important?

The passage is talking about her discovery of NGF because it opened up the world of biochemistry's eyes to this whole class of chemicals similar to NGF called neurotrophic factors (or cell-growth factors).

choices.text: Partly as a result of Levi-Montalcini’s research, it has been found that NGF and other neurotrophic factors are produced only by tissues to which nerves are already connected and that the presence of these factors is necessary for the health and proper functioning of nervous systems.
choices.tag: Too Strong: only / Wrong Emphasis: what produces NGF
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is,

*it's been found that NGF and other neurotrophic factors are produced only by tissues to which nerves are already connected, and these factors need to be present for the health and proper functioning of nervous systems.*

Levi-Montalcini doesn't appear in the main clause, despite her seeming like a very central part of the passage, not just a throwaway intro "**partly** as a result of her research".

It seems like the restrictive claim that NGF is produced **only** by tissues is contradicted in the 3rd paragraph, where it says, "It has been determined that [NGF] is present in many tissues and biological fluids, and that is especially concentrated in some organs".

choices.text: NGF, a chemical that was discovered by Levi-Montalcini, directs the growth of nerve cells toward the cells with which they must connect and ensures the survival of those nerve cells throughout the life of the organism except when the organism produces anti-NGF antibodies.
choices.explanation:
This is another answer that puts Levi-Montalcini in the background. And it centers on the specific things we learned about NGF, without capturing the idea that discovering NGF open our eyes to a whole new class of agents like it.

There is *definitely* no reason that anti-NGF antibodies should be making any appearance in our main point answer. They were brought up only in the final sentence as a very inconsequential detail. A lot of Main Point questions have a trap answer that overvalues the last thing students heard in the passage.

Finally, this says that NGF "ensures the survival of cells" where the passage just said that it is **necessary** to the continued survival of cells.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, the author would be most likely to believe that Levi-Montalcini's discovery of NGF is noteworthy primarily because it

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
In the first paragraph it gives Levi-Montalcini credit for discovering the first neurotrophic factor, which it says was a crucial development in the history of biochemistry.

The final paragraph says that Levi-Montalcini and others learned a bunch of specific stuff about NGF, but nothing in that last paragraph sounds as "noteworthy" as **crucial development in the history of biochemistry**.

So let's be flexible but anticipate that we're probably being tested on the first paragraph's two sentences.

choices.text: paved the way for more specific knowledge of the processes governing the development of the nervous system
choices.explanation:
This isn't super tempting on a first pass, but "paved the way" matches up well with "a crucial development" (in the 1st), and with "Through her work and other subsequent research, it has been determined" (in the 3rd).

Before Levi-Montalcini, we didn't even know there was such a thing as cell-growth factors or neurotrophic factors. She hypothesized that a developing nervous system produces many more nerve cells than are finally required and the "keepers" are the ones that end up in tissue supplied with nerves.

In the 3rd paragraph, we hear that her research on NGF helped us understand how neurotrophic chemicals direct the developing nerve processes toward the correct target cells.

choices.text: demonstrated that a then new laboratory technique could yield important and unanticipated experimental results
choices.explanation:
This answer is making it seem like Rita's main contribution was using the new technique of tissue culture, but that is not why she is being spotlighted in this passage.

Her discovery of NGF is definitely the more central accomplishment.

choices.text: confirmed the hypothesis that many of a developing organism’s immature nerve cells are normally programmed to die
choices.explanation:
The passage doesn't make it sound like prior to Rita's work, there was some hypothesis circling through the scientific community that many immature nerve cells are programed to die, and then she came along and confirmed it.

The second paragraph says that her research began with *her* hypothesis that many immature nerve cells are programmed to die.

And her confirmation of this fact is not the main event. As she was conducting research trying to confirm this hypothesis of hers, she accidentally stumbled on NGF, and *that* discovery revolutionized biochemistry.

choices.text: indicated that this substance stimulates observable biochemical reactions in the tissues of different species
choices.explanation:
This is a very vague idea ... many, many substances (for example, Vitamin C, nicotine, ibuprofen) will stimulate observable biochemical reactions in the tissues of different species.

So, sure, NGF will also do so, but that's far too generic of a "discovery".

choices.text: identified a specific substance, produced by mouse tumors, that can be used to stimulate nerve cell growth
choices.explanation:
This answer describes what's going on in the 2nd paragraph, where Rita is doing her specific research on chick embryos and mouse tumors.

She does identify a specific substance responsible for the nerve cell growth, the protein she names NGF.

But the primary significance of Rita's work is where the field of biochemistry goes from there. Once she makes them aware of such things as neurotrophic / cell-growth factors, they start to learn more about how these chemicals influence the development and operation of the nervous system.

questions.prompt: The primary function of the third paragraph of the passage in relation to the second paragraph is to

choices.text: indicate that conclusions referred to in the second paragraph, though essentially correct, require further verification
indicate that conclusions referred to in the second paragraph have been undermined by subsequently obtained evidence
indicate ways in which conclusions referred to in the second paragraph have been further corroborated and refined
describe subsequent discoveries of substances analogous to the substance discussed in the second paragraph
indicate that experimental procedures discussed in the second paragraph have been supplanted by more precise techniques described in the third paragraph

questions.prompt: Information in the passage most strongly supports which one of the following?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
There's no way to pre-game this question stem. On our first pass through the answers, let's be wary of anything that seems *Too Strong*, seems to be making an *Overly Broad Comparison*, bringing up something unmentioned or *Out of Scope,* or otherwise seeming to go against the passage.

We need to be able to match up the answer we're picking with some supporting lines from the text.

choices.text: Nerve cells in excess of those that are needed by the organism in which they develop eventually produce anti-NGF antibodies to suppress the effects of NGF.
choices.explanation:
This answer is saying that the extra nerve cells made when an organism is developing later produce anti-NGF antibodies. We never heard anything like that.

The passage never identifies ****any**** source of anti-NGF antibodies. It just says in the final sentence that the types of nerve cells that are affected by NGF can also be killed by anti-NGF antibodies.

choices.text: Nerve cells that grow in the absence of NGF are less numerous than, but qualitatively identical to, those that grow in the presence of NGF.
choices.explanation: We don't know anything about nerve cells that grow in the absence of NGF. The final sentence of the passage implies that such cells may exist, because it allows for "types of nerve cells that ****aren't**** affected by NGF", but we don't know anything about them and so we certainly can't sign off on the extreme idea that they are qualitatively ****identical**** to nerve cells that are affected by NGF.

choices.text: Few of the nerve cells that connect with target cells toward which NGF directs them are needed by the organism in which they develop.
choices.explanation:
This answer says that most of the nerve cells that are directed by NGF to connect with target cells are ****not**** needed by the organism?

Where would we get that most of NGF's work in patching nerve cells to target cells is useless, unneeded work?

choices.text: Some of the nerve cells that grow in the presence of NGF are eventually converted to other types of living tissue by neurotrophic factors.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: converted to other tissue
choices.explanation: The passage never talks about any nerve cells being converted into other types of living tissue.

choices.text: Some of the nerve cells that grow in an embryo do not connect with any particular target cells.
choices.explanation:
In the 2nd sentence of the 2nd paragraph, it says that,
*when embryos are in the process of forming their nervous systems, they produce many more nerve cells than are finally required, the number that survives eventually adjusting itself to the volume of tissue to be supplied with nerves*.

So if a body makes 1 million nerve cells but only 600,000 of them are required, then the other 400,000 die off.

The 2nd to last sentence of the passage explains that "NGF serves to direct the developing nerve processes toward the correct, specific *target* cells with which they must connect".

So by putting these two thoughts together, it sounds like we make 1 million nerve cells. The NGF helps attach all these wires to the tissues that need connection. Then there are extra nerve cells that die-off, because they weren't needed to connect with any particular target cells.

questions.prompt: The passage describes a specific experiment that tested which one of the following hypotheses?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
What experiments did we hear about (and what were they designed to test)?

In the beginning of the 2nd paragraph, Rita has a hypothesis and then "in order to confirm this theory, she conducted research". So that experiment was testing the hypothesis that

- many of the immature nerve cells produced in the development of an organism are normally programmed to die

A couple sentences later, we hear about "a further phase of the ****experimentation****". What hypothesis was this testing? It "began with her observation that X", and then she *theorized* (i.e. hypothesized) this:

- a chemical produced by the tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth

The following sentence refers back to it as "this ****hypothesis****".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
The two hypotheses we identified seem to be only two mentioned in the passage. So let's look for either of these:

- many of the immature nerve cells produced in the development of an organism are normally programmed to die

- a chemical produced by the tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth

choices.text: A certain kind of mouse tumor produces a chemical that stimulates the growth of nerve cells.
choices.explanation:
This sounds like the 2nd hypothesis we were looking for:

- many of the immature nerve cells produced in the development of an organism are normally programmed to die

****- a chemical produced by the tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth****

Was that a mouse tumor? Yes, she observed that *the development of nerves in chick embryos could be stimulated by implanting a certain variety of mouse tumor in the embryos.*

She then hypothesized that *a chemical produced by the [mouse] tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth.*

choices.text: Developing embryos initially grow many more nerve cells than they will eventually require.
choices.explanation:
This sounds like it's in the neighborhood of the first hypothesis:

****- many of the immature nerve cells produced in the development of an organism are normally programmed to die****

- a chemical produced by the tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth

But this answer doesn't capture the idea of "normally programmed to die". In fact from this answer we have no idea that these extra nerve cells do die; it's just as likely that they hang around uselessly.

This isn't a good enough match for "many immature nerve cells are programmed to die".

choices.text: In addition to NGF, there are several other important neurotrophic factors regulating cell survival and function.
choices.explanation:
This doesn't sound remotely like either of the two hypotheses:

- many of the immature nerve cells produced in the development of an organism are normally programmed to die

- a chemical produced by the tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth
Neither of them talked about NGF or other neurotrophic factors.

choices.text: Certain organs contain NGF in concentrations much higher than in the surrounding tissue.
choices.explanation:
This doesn't sound remotely like either of the two hypotheses:

- many of the immature nerve cells produced in the development of an organism are normally programmed to die

- a chemical produced by the tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth

Neither of them talked about NGF or organs or tissue.

choices.text: Certain nerve cells are supplied with NGF by the muscle cells to which they are connected.
choices.explanation:
This doesn't sound remotely like either of the two hypotheses:

- many of the immature nerve cells produced in the development of an organism are normally programmed to die

- a chemical produced by the tumors was responsible for the observed nerve growth

Neither of them talked about NGF or muscle cells.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since this is a totally *Undefined Target*, there's nothing to do up front.

On a first pass through answers, we'll bail quickly from anything that seems to have a common trap form, like *Too Strong, Unknown Comparison, Out of Scope*, or *Opposite*.

choices.text: Some of the effects that the author describes as occurring in Levi-Montalcini’s culture of chick embryo extract were due to neurotrophic factors other than NGF.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: other than NGF
choices.explanation:
The passage tells us that other neurotrophic factors have been discovered, other than NGF.

But NGF was the factor discovered by Levi-Montalcini in her chick experiment. The final sentence of the 2nd paragraph says:

*Further research identified **a specific substance** contributed by the mouse tumors that was responsible for the effects: NGF.*

choices.text: Although NGF was the first neurotrophic factor to be identified, some other such factors are now more thoroughly understood.
choices.explanation:
We know that other neurotrophic factors have been discovered, but there isn't any text that makes a comparison about any of them being *more thoroughly* understood than is NGF.

The final paragraph tells us a lot about NGF, too, so it seems like NGF is pretty well understood.

choices.text: In her research in the 1940s and 1950s, Levi-Montalcini identified other neurotrophic factors in addition to NGF.
choices.explanation:
We only ever hear about Levi-Montalcini discovering NGF.

The first sentence of the final paragraph says that NGF was the first of many cell-growth factors to be found, but it doesn't say or suggest that Levi-Montalcini found any of these other factors.

The following sentence returns to talking about Levi-Montalcini because the rest of the final paragraph tells us all that we now know about NGF, some of which we learned from Levi-Montalcini's research in the 40s / 50s.

choices.text: Some neurotrophic factors other than NGF perform functions that are not specifically identified in the passage.
choices.explanation:
This is as obnoxious as *Inference + Undefined Target* can get. They're just asking us to find a needle-in-a-haystack.

And sometimes that needle is found early on, in one of the "throwaway" details we might read in the 1st paragraph.

The very first sentence says that the survival of nerve cells is regulated by chemicals known as neurotrophic factors.

It also says that nerve cells' performance of some specialized functions is regulated by chemicals known as neurotrophic factors.

We only hear about NGF in the passage, and it regulates the survival of nerve cells. So presumably these other neurotrophic factors are involved in regulating the performance of some specialized functions of nerve cells. But those functions are not specifically identified by the passage.

choices.text: The effects of NGF that Levi-Montalcini noted in her chick embryo experiment are also caused by other neurotrophic factors not discussed in the passage.
choices.explanation:
We don't have any evidence that the other neurotrophic factors also have the effect of controlling the survival of nerve cells.

The first sentence says that "survival of cells as well as performance of specialized functions is regulated by neurotrophic factors". That doesn't mean that all neurotrophic factors do both things.

We can say "color of eyes as well as height are regulated by genes". That doesn't mean that every type of gene regulates eye color and height. That sentence can just mean that some genes handle eye color, other handle height.

passages.title: The Modern Movement
passages.text:
The proponents of the Modern Movement in architecture considered that, compared with the historical styles that it replaced, Modernist architecture more accurately reflected the functional spirit of twentieth-century technology and was better suited to the newest building methods. It is ironic, then, that the Movement fostered an ideology of design that proved to be at odds with the way buildings were really built.

The tenacious adherence of Modernist architects and critics to this ideology was in part responsible for the Movement’s decline. Originating in the 1920s as a marginal, almost bohemian art movement, the Modern Movement was never very popular with the public, but this very lack of popular support produced in Modernist architects a high-minded sense of mission—not content merely to interpret the needs of the client, these architects now sought to persuade, to educate, and, if necessary, to dictate. By 1945 the tenets of the Movement had come to dominate mainstream architecture, and by the early 1950s, to dominate architectural criticism—architects whose work seemed not to advance the evolution of the Modern Movement tended to be dismissed by proponents of Modernism. On the other hand, when architects were identified as innovators—as was the case with Otto Wagner and the young Frank Lloyd Wright—attention was drawn to only those features of their work that were “Modern”; other aspects were conveniently ignored.

The decline of the Modern Movement later in the twentieth century occurred partly as a result of Modernist architects’ ignorance of building methods, and partly because Modernist architects were reluctant to admit that their concerns were chiefly aesthetic. Moreover, the building industry was evolving in a direction Modernists had not anticipated: it was more specialized and the process of construction was much more fragmented than in the past. Up until the twentieth century, construction had been carried out by a relatively small number of tradespeople, but as the building industry evolved, buildings came to be built by many specialized subcontractors working independently. The architect’s design not only had to accommodate a sequence of independent operations, but now had to reflect the allowable degree of inaccuracy of the different trades. However, one of the chief construction ideals of the Modern Movement was to “honestly” expose structural materials such as steel and concrete. To do this and still produce a visually acceptable interior called for an unrealistically high level of craftmanship. Exposure of a building’s internal structural elements, if it could be achieved at all, could only be accomplished at considerable cost—hence the well-founded reputation of Modern architecture as prohibitively expensive.

As Postmodern architects recognized, the need to expose structural elements imposed unnecessary limitations on building design. The unwillingness of architects of the Modern Movement to abandon their ideals contributed to the decline of interest in the Modern Movement.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The rise and decline of Modernist architecture, focusing on its ideals versus practical realities in building methods.

**Framework**

Old / New

**Main Point**

Although the Modern Movement in architecture aimed to express the technological and functional spirit of the twentieth century, its rigid ideology eventually conflicted with actual building practices, leading to its decline as Postmodern architecture recognized and addressed these limitations. ("It is ironic, then, that the Movement fostered an ideology of design that proved to be at odds with the way buildings were really built." - End of P1 "The unwillingness of architects of the Modern Movement to abandon their ideals contributed to the decline of interest in the Modern Movement." - End of P4)

**P1: Introduction—Modernist Ideals vs. Reality**

Modernist architecture was supposed to match the spirit of new technology and be suitable for modern building techniques, but ironically, its design ideology didn't fit well with how buildings were actually constructed.

**P2: Ascent of Modernism and Its Blind Spots**

Modernism started out as a rebel movement, but soon took over mainstream architecture. Its proponents became elitist, caring more about pushing their vision than serving clients, and critics often misrepresented architects' work by ignoring non-Modern features.

**P3: Why Modernism Declined—Practical & Conceptual Issues**

Modernist architects misunderstood real construction processes and wouldn't admit that their work was mostly about looks, not function. As the construction industry became more specialized, it was nearly impossible to build Modernist designs "honestly" without extreme expense and impractical expectations.

**P4: Postmodernism’s Response & Modernism’s Fall**

Postmodern architects saw that exposing structural elements (a Modernist ideal) just made things harder and less flexible, and Modernists’ refusal to adapt or let go of these ideals helped make their style unpopular and outdated.

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
If we CTRL + F or scan for keywords in "exposing structural materials", we find it towards the end of the 3rd paragraph.

Is there any author opinion in that area?

Yes, the author says that in order to achieve the Modern architects' ideal of exposing structural materials "*and still produce a visually acceptable interior called for an **unrealistically** high level of craftsmanship."*

She also says that if you could achieve this standard at all, it "*could only be accomplished at **considerable** cost - hence the **well-founded** reputation of Modern architecture as prohibitively expensive*".

So overall we get the author saying that this idea was not feasible; it was unrealistic; it was too expensive.

Let's look for something reinforcing those sentiments.

choices.text: The repudiation of the ideal by some of these architects undermined its validity.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: repudiation of the ideal
choices.explanation:
Nothing at the end of the 3rd paragraph says that some Modern architects **repudiated** (i.e. rejected) the ideal.

It just says that the ideal was an unrealistically expensive one to try to execute.

choices.text: The ideal was rarely achieved because of its lack of popular appeal.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: lack of popular appeal
choices.explanation:
Nothing at the end of the 3rd paragraph says that *people didn't like the look* of exposed structural materials.

It just says that the ideal was an unrealistically expensive one to try to execute.

choices.text: The ideal was unrealistic because most builders were unwilling to attempt it.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: unwilling to attempt / Too Strong: most
choices.explanation:
Nothing at the end of the 3rd paragraph says that **more than 50%** of builders were *unwilling* to try having exposed structural materials such as steel and concrete.

It just says that the ideal was an unrealistically *expensive* one to try to execute.

choices.text: The ideal originated in the work of Otto Wagner and Frank Lloyd Wright.
choices.explanation:
Nothing at the end of the 3rd paragraph talks about Wagner or Wright. Those are just examples of architects who were famous and innovative (whom the Modern Movement tried to claim as their own).

Since the passage suggests that Wagner and Wright weren't even truly part of the Modern Movement, we definitely have no grounds for claiming that they **invented** this ideal of exposed structural materials.

choices.text: The ideal arose from aesthetic rather than practical concerns.
choices.explanation:
This causal claim was never stated, but we're being tested here on what's implied.

Since the end of the 3rd paragraph is telling us that this ideal called for an **unrealistically** high level of craftsmanship and required such **considerable** cost that it would be **prohibitively** expensive, we can tell that this ideal was very, very *im*practical.

Practical concerns are all about what's realistic, what's feasible, what makes sense given actual limitations and constraints.

And since the author is telling us how crazy-town this ideal was to have exposed structural materials, we can tell it definitely **wasn't** motivated by practical concerns.

We have to speculate that it otherwise arose from aesthetic concerns, but given that architects are artists and given that we're told in the first line of this 3rd paragraph that, "Modernist architects were reluctant to admit that their concerns were **chiefly aesthetic**", we have good grounds for finding this answer a reasonable inference.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
What framework did we use for this passage? Why was the author writing about the Modern Movement?

She definitely had some snarky attitude towards the movement, so we might think *Challenge Position*.

But the final sentence of the 1st paragraph seems to give us a Framing Idea that provides a summary of the story the rest of the passage tells:

*The Movement fostered an ideology of design that proved to be at odds with the way buildings were really built*.

The 2nd paragraph adds that Modernist architects' tenacious adherence to this ideology was also partly responsible for its decline.

The 2nd paragraph goes on to explain how the Modernists became the trendy new thing and insisted everyone else join them.

The 3rd paragraph revisits the idea that "Modernist architecture was at odds with the way building were really built" / "the decline occurred partly as a result of Modernist architects' ignorance of building methods".

So the passage seems to mainly be a *Highlight Noteworthy* passage, since it's telling a story that falls underneath an umbrella claim in the first paragraph. The 2nd and 3rd paragraphs both tell the story of why Modernism was ultimately a bad idea the world phased out.

choices.text: analyzing the failure of a movement
choices.explanation:
This aligns with our Most Valuable Sentences.

(end of 1st):
*The Movement fostered an ideology that proved **at odds** with the way buildings were built*

(beginning of 2nd)
*The tenacious adherence of Modernist architects was in part **responsible** for the Movement's **decline**.*

(beginning of 3rd)
*The **decline** of the Modern Movement later in the 20th century occurred **partly as a result** of Modernist architects' ignorance of building methods.*

choices.text: predicting the future course of a movement
choices.explanation: Nothing in the passage discusses the future of Modernism.

choices.text: correcting a misunderstanding about a movement
choices.explanation:
The passage isn't framed around a misconception that we're trying to correct.

It's not like some people think Modernism died because of X, but the author is explaining to them it really died because of Y and Z.

choices.text: anticipating possible criticism of a movement
choices.explanation:
This answer seems to have the tense all wrong.

The Modern Movement already happened. It already received its criticisms. It already declined by the end of the 1900's.

So the author isn't writing this passage to predict what people might say critically about the movement in the future.

choices.text: contrasting incompatible viewpoints about a movement
choices.explanation:
The word "incompatible" basically means *contradictory*. Were there contradictory views about Modernism in this passage that the author was trying to contrast?

No, none of the views contradict.

For example, the Modernists like to "honestly expose structural materials such as steel and concrete". A criticism of Modernism is that "doing so with a visually acceptable result requires a high level of craftmanship".

Those do not contradict each other. A contradiction would be "honestly exposing structural materials **doesn't** require a high level of craftmanship".
